opus-5.5.text:
I think the industry is moving toward a clear division of labor, a bit like what we saw in the PC and smartphone eras. No single company is going to do everything well, so you'll see roughly three or four types of players, each focused on what it's best at.

First, the **technology providers**: the companies building the autonomous driving stack, meaning the perception, prediction, planning, the large models behind it, plus the simulation and data closed loop. That is very capital- and talent-intensive, and only a handful of companies globally will be able to do it at the highest level. It's similar to how only a few companies make operating systems or chips.

Second, the **vehicle manufacturers**. Robotaxis need vehicles designed for autonomy from the start, with redundant braking, steering, power, sensors, and compute built in rather than bolted on. OEMs are very good at manufacturing at scale, controlling cost, and ensuring quality and safety certification. I don't think most autonomous driving companies should be building cars themselves, and I don't think most carmakers can build a world-class driving stack. So partnership is the natural model.

Third, the **operators and fleet platforms**: the ride-hailing companies, mobility service providers, sometimes taxi companies or even local governments. They know the users, the demand patterns, dispatching, pricing, and the day-to-day work of cleaning, charging, maintenance, insurance, and customer service. Operations is often underestimated, but at scale it determines whether the unit economics work.

And then there's a fourth layer that matters a lot in China in particular: **infrastructure and government**. That means vehicle-road-cloud coordination, roadside sensing, high-definition maps, 5G or C-V2X connectivity, and the regulatory framework, including licensing, liability, and data rules. Here the public sector plays a much bigger role than in many other industries.

So my view is that the winners won't be the ones who try to own the whole chain, but the ones who define a clear position and build an open ecosystem around it. Of course, in the early stage some companies do have to be vertically integrated, because the ecosystem doesn't exist yet and you have to prove the whole system works end to end. But as the technology matures and costs come down, I expect specialization to increase, and the industry will look more like a layered structure with platforms, hardware, and services.

One more point: I believe robotaxi is really the starting point. The same technology will extend to logistics, trucking, buses, and eventually personal vehicles. The division of roles we establish in robotaxi will probably shape the entire smart transportation industry for the next ten to twenty years.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes vehicle manufacturers from operators and says partnership between them is the natural model.

r002.rationale: It identifies technology providers that build the autonomous driving stack as a distinct player type.

r003.rationale: It says some companies may be vertically integrated early on and must prove the whole system end to end, indicating one company may span manufacturing and robotaxi operations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the robotaxi business will eventually settle into a fairly clear three-layer structure, and no single company will do everything.

The first layer is the technology provider, the company that builds the autonomous driving system itself, the "brain." That is the perception, planning, the full-stack software, plus the data infrastructure and the simulation and safety validation behind it. This is extremely capital-intensive and talent-intensive, and it has strong scale effects, because the more miles you accumulate, the better your system becomes. So I expect only a handful of players globally will survive at this layer, maybe three to five in China, and a similar number in the US.

The second layer is the vehicle manufacturer. OEMs know how to build cars at scale, with quality, cost control, and safety certification that a software company simply cannot replicate overnight. In the long run, a robotaxi is not a regular car with sensors bolted on. It needs to be designed from the ground up for autonomy, with redundancy in braking, steering, and power. So the OEMs have a very natural role, and their relationship with the technology providers will be a deep partnership rather than a simple supplier arrangement.

The third layer is the operator, the one who actually runs the fleet and faces the customer. This includes the ride-hailing platforms, which already have the demand side, the users, the dispatching algorithms, the pricing, and the city-level operating experience. It also includes fleet management, charging, cleaning, maintenance, insurance, and dealing with local regulators. This is a very local, very operational business.

Now, the interesting question is who captures the most value. I believe the technology layer and the demand layer will have the strongest positions, and the hardware layer will be more like today's smartphone supply chain, important but with thinner margins. Some companies will try to be vertically integrated, like Tesla, or Waymo to some extent. Others, like us at Baidu with Apollo Go, started vertically integrated out of necessity, because the ecosystem did not exist yet, but over time we want to open up and work with OEMs and operators.

So my view is that in the early stage, vertical integration wins, because you need to control everything to get the product to work. In the mature stage, specialization wins, because each layer has very different economics and competencies. The companies that succeed will be the ones that know when to make that transition.

r001.rationale: It describes vehicle manufacturers and fleet operators as distinct layers, with OEMs partnering with operators.

r002.rationale: It identifies autonomous-driving technology providers as a separate layer that supplies the system, software, and supporting technology.

r003.rationale: It says some companies will be vertically integrated and that early integration means controlling everything, which includes manufacturing vehicles and operating services across the described layers.

astra-6.text:
I think the robotaxi business will evolve into an ecosystem, with different companies playing different roles. Some will develop the autonomous driving technology—the software, computing platform, and intelligence. Automakers will design and manufacture vehicles with those capabilities integrated. And operators will manage the fleets, maintain the cars, and provide the service to passengers.

In the early stages, a company may need to do all of these things itself to make the system work. But as the technology matures, I expect more specialization and more partnerships. Building a reliable autonomous driver, manufacturing a vehicle, and operating a transportation service require quite different capabilities. A few companies may remain vertically integrated, but I don't think every company needs to own the whole chain.

r001.rationale: It describes automakers making vehicles and separate operators managing fleets and passenger service, with specialization and partnerships expected.

r002.rationale: It identifies companies developing autonomous-driving software, computing platforms, and intelligence as a distinct role, integrated into vehicles by automakers.

r003.rationale: It says a company may need to do all the listed activities itself, including manufacturing vehicles and operating fleets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the robotaxi business will evolve into an ecosystem, with different companies focusing on different layers. Automakers will build vehicles designed for autonomous driving. Autonomous driving companies will provide the technology—the software, computing platform, and the ability to operate safely without a driver. Then there will be companies responsible for fleet operations, maintenance, charging, and customer service, as well as platforms that connect passengers with vehicles.

Some companies will integrate several of those roles, especially in the early stages, because they need to make the whole system work. But over time, I expect more specialization and partnerships. Being good at building a car doesn’t automatically mean you’re good at developing autonomous driving technology or operating a transportation service.

The key question is whether those partners can deliver a service that is safe, reliable, and economically sustainable. That will determine which business models succeed.

r001.rationale: It assigns vehicle building to automakers and fleet operations and customer service to other companies, describing distinct roles.

r002.rationale: It identifies autonomous driving companies as a separate role providing software, computing platforms, and autonomous driving capability.

r003.rationale: It says some companies may integrate several roles, but does not clearly state that one company may combine vehicle manufacturing with robotaxi service operation.
